title: Technical Quickplay: Canary + Fallback Economics Pocket (Draft)
content:
Purpose
- Short, action-first pocket doc to help technical sellers run rapid qualification, propose canary + fallback configurations, and quickly translate performance targets to cost estimates. Not a full deck — intentionally dense, skimmable, and copy-paste friendly for Slack/email.

Audience
- Solutions engineers, AE technical sellers, CS pre-sales engineers.

Status / how to use this draft
- Draft: put into seller Slack channel for feedback, test in two upcoming demos (Acct: Typhon Health, Pilot: docs summarizer).
- TODO: add 2 customer-specific example prompts for Typhon and FinTrust.

One-liner (elevator)
- If latency spikes or reserved capacity fails, keep product alive by routing to a lower-cost but compatible variant with controlled quality rollback — this checklist helps you pick the variant, estimate per-minute cost, and define rollback thresholds for the canary.

Quick outcomes sellers should deliver after a 15-minute call
- Confirm SLOs: p95 latency target, acceptable error rates, throughput (rps)
- Identify primary model baseline and one fallback variant (quantized/shorter-context/cheaper model)
- Propose canary traffic % and duration; calculate worst-case incremental spend if fallback is used for X hours
- Document rollout policy (who is notified, auto-fallback thresholds, manual override channel)

Key concepts (short)
- Canary: small % of traffic or subset of routes to new model/version to validate real-world performance. Keep short (5–60 min) for functional checks; longer for long-tail quality tests.
- Fallback: explicit route to alternate model(s) when capacity, latency, or quality regressions occur. Should be compatible (same API shape) and graded (tiered).
- Variant types: quantized (smaller memory/cheaper per-token), lower-context (shorter seq length), architecture-lite (smaller model family), or cached-prefetch (use stronger caching on common prefixes).

Canary + Fallback Matrix (copy to email)
- Inputs: baseline_model, fallback_candidate, expected_q_loss, fallback_type, estimated_cost_ratio
- Example row (pasteable):
  baseline: redwood-rlhf-13b-full, fallback: redwood-13b-q4_0, expected_quality_delta: ~2–4% (semantic tasks), fallback_type: quantized, est_cost_ratio: 0.6
  baseline: open-llama-70b, fallback: open-llama-13b, expected_quality_delta: 8–12% (long-context summarization), fallback_type: downsize, est_cost_ratio: 0.35

Technical qualification checklist (5m script)
- Workload: Is it single-turn generation (embeds/answers) or multi-turn chat with KV cache persistence?
- Token profile: average input tokens, average output tokens, max sequence length observed in logs
- Concurrency: peak rps and burst characteristics (how many parallel open requests)
- SLOs: p50/p90/p95 latency targets, error tolerances, acceptable fallback duration
- Data constraints: regulated PII? Need private deployment or dedicated?

Objection handling (brief scripts)
- "Will fallback break my app?" -> Answer: We choose compatible variants (same call/response shape). Start with a short canary window to verify outputs. If outputs deviate beyond the agreed threshold we rollback automatically.
- "Why not just overprovision?" -> Answer: Overprovisioning buys capacity but not predictability for global incidents. Canary + fallback allows graceful degradation with bounded cost and minimal data exposure.
- "Does fallback change embeddings/semantic search?" -> Answer: It can. For retrieval workflows we recommend a model-store approach: keep embeddings pinned to a single stable model; route only generation calls to fallback.

Cost quick math (cheat formulas)
- Per-minute cost estimate = (avg_output_tokens + avg_input_tokens) * per_token_price * requests_per_minute
- Worst-case incremental cost for fallback = (fallback_cost_per_min / baseline_cost_per_min - 1) * baseline_commit_cost * hours_of_fallback
- Quick number sample (for talking): baseline redwood-13b-full = $0.020 / 1k tokens (gen), fallback = redwood-13b-q4_0 = $0.012 / 1k tokens. For 10 rps, avg 200 tokens total => baseline ≈ $0.04 / min, fallback ≈ $0.024 / min, savings ≈ $0.016 / min (≈ $23/day if used continuously).

Canary configuration templates (pick one)
- Functional canary (fast validation): 1–2% traffic, 15 minutes, check error rates & basic semantic sanity.
- Quality canary (longer tail): 5% traffic, 2–4 hours, run prompt set of 20 critical prompts; evaluate precision by human spot checks or automated evals.
- Safety canary (sensitive domains): 0.5% traffic, continuous but very narrow sample (non-production users or internal test accounts).

Rollout + alerting play (practical)
- Triggers for fallback: p95 latency > SLO * 2 for 3 consecutive minutes OR error rate > 1% for 2 min OR resource saturation (GPU mem pressure alert).
- Notifications: channel #sre-inference, tag on-call SRE and AE. Create incident if fallback persists > 30 minutes.
- Automatic vs manual: prefer auto-fallback for latency/resource triggers; prefer manual for quality regressions. Document the exact toggles in the customer rollout doc.

Sample mini-checklist to paste in Jira/ticket for pilot
- [ ] Define baseline model + config (quantization, kv cache settings)
- [ ] Define fallback candidate(s) + expected quality delta
- [ ] Canary % and duration defined + test prompts (10–20)
- [ ] Define alert thresholds and notification channels
- [ ] Cost estimate for 24/72/168 hour fallback scenario
- [ ] Run internal dry-run with synthetic load

Seller-ready battle snippets (copyable)
- Speed-first: "We can keep your app live with sub-second fallbacks while we mitigate upstream issues — usually with a small quality tradeoff that we quantify up front."
- Cost-first: "Fallbacks are designed to limit spend surprises — we estimate worst-case incremental charge and set auto-stop thresholds."
- Platform-first: "Same API, same telemetry — your observability and tracing are preserved across canary and fallback so you can trace regressions to prompts or code."

Evaluation prompt set (starter)
- 1–5: short QA prompts (fact lookup)
- 6–10: multi-turn summarization snippets (3 turns each)
- 11–15: safety/regulatory phrases check (PII redaction quality)
- 16–20: edge-case long-context concatenation (customer-specific)

Notes to self / open questions (insert after trials)
- Need two concrete examples showing user-visible delta (Typhon Health: clinical note summarization — expected quality delta acceptable?; FinTrust: compliance Q&A — likely not acceptable for certain fallback types).
- Add visuals: small bar chart showing cost ratio and p95 latency for baseline vs fallback.
- Consolidate with engineering on exact alert formula names (SRE uses alert IDs, add them here before shipping).

Appendix: common fallback candidates (quick reference)
- redwood-13b-q4_0 — good cost/quality balance, safe for many generation tasks
- redwood-7b-quant — best for cost-limited burst handling, expect more quality variance on long-coherence tasks
- open-llama-13b — useful if customer already uses open models and wants predictable licensing

Next steps (owner: Ivy)
- Iterate with SEs after two customer pilots (target: 2026-03-15).
- Convert high-priority bits into a 1-page PDF cheat card for field.

End of draft.

Editor notes: keep this under 2 pages when converted to a slide or cheat PDF. Emphasize copy-paste sections for sellers, and keep the math small and memorable.
